mcqs.q: A colloid is a mixture that is:
opts: Intermediate between a suspension and a solution (particles 1–1000 nm), e.g. milk
mcqs.explain: Colloids (1–1000 nm) lie between solutions (0.01–1 nm) and suspensions (>1000 nm).

mcqs.q: A colloidal system whose dispersion medium is water is called a:
mcqs.explain: When the dispersion medium is water, the colloid is a hydrocolloid (agar, alginate).

mcqs.q: The two physical forms of a hydrocolloid are:
mcqs.explain: Hydrocolloids exist as a sol (liquid) or a gel (jelly).

mcqs.q: A REVERSIBLE hydrocolloid changes sol ⇌ gel by:
mcqs.explain: Reversible = physical (temperature): heat gel → sol, cool sol → gel. Irreversible = chemical (sol → gel).

mcqs.q: The loss of water from a gel by evaporation or exudation is termed:
mcqs.explain: Syneresis = water loss; imbibition = water uptake. Both distort the impression.

mcqs.q: If a water-deficient gel is placed in contact with water, it absorbs water by:
mcqs.explain: Imbibition is water uptake by a gel; this is why a soaking-wet storage towel distorts alginate.

mcqs.q: Agar (ADA No. 11) is best described as a:
mcqs.explain: Agar is an organic hydrophilic colloid from seaweed — reversible and elastic (sol ⇌ gel with temperature).

mcqs.q: In the 3-chamber hydrocolloid conditioner, the first (liquefying) step is performed at:
mcqs.explain: Liquefy at 100°C ×10 min (gel→sol), store at 65°C, temper at 46°C ×3 min.

mcqs.q: Agar impressions use rim-lock trays because:
opts: Agar does not adhere to the tray, so beading/rim-lock mechanically retains it (with water cooling)
mcqs.explain: Rim-lock beading retains the non-adhering agar, and water circulation (18–21°C) gels it.

mcqs.q: Alginate (ADA No. 18) is:
opts: An irreversible, elastic hydrocolloid — the most widely used dental impression material
mcqs.explain: Alginate is an irreversible elastic hydrocolloid from brown seaweed, and the most widely used impression material.

mcqs.q: The largest component (by weight) of alginate powder is:
mcqs.explain: Diatomaceous earth (~60%) is the filler; potassium alginate ~15% and calcium sulphate ~16% drive the set; sodium phosphate ~2% is the retarder.

mcqs.q: Alginate powder is best mixed using a:
opts: Vigorous figure-of-eight motion, swiping against the sides of a plaster bowl
Gentle circular stir in a metal cup
Single sweep with a wax knife
mcqs.explain: A vigorous figure-of-eight against the bowl dissolves all the alginate to a smooth, creamy, non-dripping mix.

mcqs.q: The recommended way to control alginate's gelation time is to alter the:
mcqs.explain: Control set with water temperature; do NOT change the W/P ratio or mixing time (these harm properties). Colder = longer, warmer = shorter.

mcqs.q: If an alginate impression must be stored before pouring, it should be:
opts: Kept in a damp (not soaking) towel or sealed bag for no more than one hour
Left dry on the bench overnight
mcqs.explain: Store ≤1 hour in a damp towel/sealed bag; a soaking-wet towel causes imbibition, and drying causes syneresis.

mcqs.q: Because alginate distorts on immersion, it is best disinfected by:
opts: Spraying and sealing in a bag for ~10 minutes
mcqs.explain: Alginate distorts if immersed, so spray-disinfect and seal ~10 min.

mcqs.q: A recognized USE of alginate is:
opts: Primary impressions for complete dentures and study/working casts
Final crown margins requiring the finest detail
mcqs.explain: Alginate is used for primary/complete-denture impressions, study and working casts, undercuts, high-saliva mouths and duplicating models.

mcqs.q: By particle size, a SOLUTION is defined by components measuring:
mcqs.explain: A colloid is intermediate at 1–1000 nm, and a suspension is greater than 1000 nm.

mcqs.q: A suspension differs from a solution in that it is:
opts: Heterogeneous — the components do not mix completely and separate
Homogeneous — the components mix thoroughly and stay mixed
mcqs.explain: Sand in water and oil in water are the examples given.

mcqs.q: A colloidal suspension of SOLID particles in a liquid is called a:
mcqs.explain: An emulsion is between two liquids, a foam is gas trapped in a liquid or solid, and an aerosol is liquid or solid dispersed in a gas.

mcqs.q: An IRREVERSIBLE hydrocolloid gel can return to the sol state only by:
opts: Reversing the original chemical reaction — which is not possible, so it cannot be reversed by heat
mcqs.explain: A reversible hydrocolloid, by contrast, changes sol to gel purely with temperature.

mcqs.q: Agar is an organic hydrophilic colloid extracted from:
mcqs.explain: Alginate is a mucus extraction from a BROWN seaweed (algae).

mcqs.q: The largest component of agar by weight is:
mcqs.explain: Agar itself is only 12.5%, which is why syneresis and imbibition matter so much.

mcqs.q: Agar is supplied in two consistencies. The SYRINGE consistency is:
opts: More fluid than the tray material and a different colour, injected around the teeth
More viscous than the tray material, loaded into the tray
The same as the tray material but pre-warmed
mcqs.explain: The tray consistency is the bulk material loaded into the water-cooled tray.

mcqs.q: In the three-chamber hydrocolloid conditioner, the LIQUEFYING chamber operates at:
mcqs.explain: Storage is at 65 °C and tempering at 46 °C for 3 minutes; 18–21 °C is the cooling water temperature in the tray.

mcqs.q: After seating an agar tray, gelation is produced by circulating water at:
mcqs.explain: This converts the sol back to a gel.

mcqs.q: Immersion disinfection of an agar impression should not exceed:
mcqs.explain: Sodium hypochlorite, iodophor or glutaraldehyde may be used.

mcqs.q: A recognised use of agar impression material is:
opts: Border moulding of a custom tray
mcqs.explain: Full-mouth impressions are its other stated use.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of agar?
opts: It needs extensive, expensive equipment and tears relatively easily
It gives a poor model surface
mcqs.explain: Good elastic properties, accurate undercut reproduction, good recovery from distortion and a good model surface are its advantages.

mcqs.q: Which component of alginate acts as the REACTOR?
mcqs.explain: Sodium phosphate is the retarder and diatomaceous earth is the filler.

mcqs.q: Alginate powder should be mixed using:
opts: A vigorous figure-of-eight motion, swiping the mix against the sides of the bowl
A gentle stirring motion to avoid incorporating air
A rotary motion in a glass slab
mcqs.explain: All the alginate must be dissolved, otherwise a good gel cannot form; the result is a smooth creamy mix that does not drip off the spatula.

mcqs.q: The ideal gelation time for alginate at room temperature (25 °C) is:
mcqs.explain: Gelation is controlled by the WATER TEMPERATURE — colder water lengthens it, warmer water shortens it — never by changing the water/powder ratio.

mcqs.q: If an alginate impression must be stored, it should be:
opts: Wrapped lightly in a wet paper towel or kept in a plastic bag, for no more than 1 hour
Immersed in water until it can be poured
Left open to the air to dry
Wrapped in a soaking wet towel to prevent syneresis
mcqs.explain: A soaking wet towel causes imbibition of water and distortion.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of alginate?
opts: It does not lose surface detail in wet mouths
It flows readily into areas the tray does not reach
It can be added to if faulty
It is not liable to distort
mcqs.explain: The other three are its stated disadvantages.

saqs.q: Distinguish a suspension, a solution and a colloid by particle size, and define a hydrocolloid.
saqs.a: SUSPENSION — heterogeneous, particles > 1000 nm, components separate (sand in water). SOLUTION — homogeneous, particles 0.01–1 nm, stays mixed (salt in water). COLLOID — intermediate, particles 1–1000 nm (milk). A HYDROCOLLOID is a colloid whose dispersion medium is WATER — agar, alginate.

ans.text: A HYDROCOLLOID is a colloid whose dispersion medium is water — e.g. agar and alginate.

saqs.q: Define syneresis and imbibition and explain their clinical relevance.
saqs.a: SYNERESIS is the LOSS of water from a gel by evaporation or exudation; IMBIBITION is the UPTAKE of water by a water-deficient gel on contact with water. Both DISTORT hydrocolloid impressions, so pour promptly and, if stored, keep in a damp (not soaking) environment for no more than one hour.

ans.text: Both distort hydrocolloid impressions — so the impression is poured promptly and, if stored, kept in a damp (not soaking) environment for no more than one hour.

saqs.q: Describe the conditioning of agar (the 3-chamber unit) and why rim-lock trays are used.
saqs.a: Agar is conditioned in a 3-CHAMBER unit — (1) LIQUEFY at 100 °C for ~10 min, converting gel → sol; (2) STORE at 65 °C; (3) TEMPER at 46 °C for ~3 min before loading. RIM-LOCK trays are used because agar DOES NOT ADHERE to the tray — the rim-lock beading retains it mechanically; water circulated at 18–21 °C for ~3 min gels it (sol → gel).

ans.text: Rim-lock trays are used because agar does not adhere to the tray — the beading on the inside edge retains it mechanically. After seating, water at 18–21 °C is circulated for ~3 min to convert sol → gel.

saqs.q: Give the two types of alginate with their working/setting times, and state how gelation time is controlled.
saqs.a: TYPE I (regular set) — working time ~2 min, setting time 2–4.5 min. TYPE II (fast set) — working time ~75 s, setting time 1–2 min; ideal gelation 2–3 min at 25 °C. GELATION is controlled by the TEMPERATURE OF THE MIXING WATER — colder lengthens and warmer shortens the set — NOT by changing the water/powder ratio or the mixing time.

ans.text: Gelation is controlled by the temperature of the mixing water — colder lengthens and warmer shortens the set. It must not be altered by changing the water/powder ratio or the mixing time.

saqs.q: List two advantages and two disadvantages of alginate.
saqs.a: ADVANTAGES (any two) — easy to mix and manipulate; dimensionally accurate if poured soon after removal; does not lose surface detail in wet mouths; wide range available; economical; records undercuts. DISADVANTAGES (any two) — does not flow well into areas the tray does not extend to; cannot be added to if faulty; liable to distort, so must be poured promptly.

saqs.q: Describe agar: its specification, nature, composition and the equipment needed to use it.
saqs.a: AGAR is A.D.A. Specification No. 11, an organic hydrophilic colloid extracted from certain seaweeds. It is REVERSIBLE, ELASTIC and of low viscosity; its reaction is agar hot → agar cold, that is SOL → GEL. COMPOSITION — water 85.5%, agar 12.5%, potassium sulphate 1.7%, borax 0.2%, alkyl benzoate 0.1%. EQUIPMENT — a 3-chamber hydrocolloid conditioner (liquefy 100 °C / 10 min; store 65 °C, where it is loaded; temper 46 °C / 3 min) and water-cooled RIM-LOCK trays, the beading retaining the material because agar does not adhere to the tray. After seating, water at 18–21 °C is circulated for 3 min to convert sol → gel.

saqs.q: Give the uses, advantages and disadvantages of alginate.
saqs.a: USES — primary impressions for complete dentures; study models and working casts; recording undercuts; mouths with excessive saliva; duplicating models. ADVANTAGES — easy to mix and manipulate; dimensionally accurate if poured soon after removal; does not lose surface detail in wet mouths; wide range available; economical. DISADVANTAGES — does not flow readily into areas the tray does not extend to; cannot be added to if faulty; liable to distort. DISINFECTION — because alginate distorts when immersed, it is disinfected by SPRAYING with glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde, sodium hypochlorite or phenol derivatives, then sealing in a plastic bag for about 10 minutes.
